newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK trade deficit narrows despite strong pound.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK trade deficit narrows despite strong pound.

text.p: Britain's global trade deficit narrowed to 671 million pounds in March, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Thursday, as the pound's recent sustained rally failed to take its expected toll on exports.
The March figure compared with a gap of 771 million pounds in February, revised up from 758 million.
The ONS said the trend in trade was erratic but the global trade deficit appeared to be narrowing.

Economists had expected the deficit to widen to 900 million pounds as strong consumer demand sucked in higher imports and sterling's 17 percent rise since August last year started to dampen demand for exports.
But in the event, both exports and imports registered slight falls. Exports fell by 2.6 percent compared with February while imports dropped by 3.2 percent.

"The main feature of the numbers is how well exports have held up despite the strength of sterling and the frequent complaints of the corporate sector that their exports are being damaged," said CIBC chief economist David Coleman.
"There will be an impact at some point but it could be well into next year before we get anything significant."
Britain's trade deficit with the rest of the European Union was 20 million pounds in March, down sharply from 321 million in February.

More up-to-date but incomplete figures for April showed a smaller than expected deficit in Britain's trade with non-EU countries of 335 million stg, compared with market expectations that it would be close to March's figure of 606 million.
Stripped of volatile trade components such as ships, aircraft, precious stones, the deficit narrowed to just 259 million pounds from 407 million in March.
Economists said there were signs of a split developing between Britain's trade position with the EU and with non-EU countries which could be attributable to the pound's performance.
"This gap is almost certainly explained by the fact that sterling has made most of its gains over the past year against the other European currencies," said HSBC economist Dharshini David.
The volume of underlying exports to the EU was unchanged over the three months to March but exports to non-EU countries jumped 5.7 percent.
David argued that although the trade deficit is continuing to narrow, there is other evidence that exporters are suffering under the weight of the exchange rate.
"It can only be a matter of time before we see export volumes slow more sharply across the board," David said.

The Confederation of British Industry said last week that manufacturers were failing to win export contracts because of the pound's strength. Its May industry survey said export demand was at its lowest level since 1993.
But if the strength of the pound represents a long-term threat to exports, it should at least help the new Labour government to deliver its objective of low inflation.
The price of underlying imports fell by 1.3 percent in the three months to March.
